newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Airlines, union leaders start talks.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Airlines, union leaders start talks.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp. and its six unions began talks on Wednesday on issues including allowing workers a free vote on a proposed 10 percent wage rollback the carrier says is essential to its survival.

Canadian's biggest unions, including the International Association of Machinists and the Canadian Auto Workers, have rejected Canadian's plans to cut wages and criticized its information meetings with thousands of company employees in the past two weeks.

But Wednesday's meeting in Vancouver came after Canadian and leaders of its biggest union, the 5,300-member IAM, agreed to discussions on a wage proposal, one of the three main parts of the Calgary-based carrier's survival plan.

The IAM had launched a complaint with Canada's federal labor board over the carrier's employee sessions, but canceled a hearing on Tuesday and agreed to the meeting with Canadian Chief Executive Kevin Benson.
Canadian, in turn, halted the information sessions.
Benson, in a statement to employees on Tuesday, acknowledged that the company's information sessions with about 6,000 workers across the country caused friction with union leadership.
"This was not our intent," he said. "And given the challenges that the company is facing, I feel that it is not in our interest to have disagreement of the content of the meeting."

Despite accepting Benson's invitation to talk, leaders of Canadian's 3,700 CAW members said they did not plan to change their call for a rejection of the wage cuts, a government bailout of the airline and re-regulation of Canada's air industry.

"It's Mr. Benson's meeting, so we're there to listen," CAW President Buzz Hargrove said in an interview. "But one thing we're not buying into is that somehow the wage cuts are going to solve his problem."

Benson has said that the survival plan, which also includes route restructurings and a C$48 million ($36 million) cut in annual service fees to AMR Corp., were not negotiable and that the company would wind up operations if all participants did not agree by a Nov. 30 deadline.
Some CAW employees in Calgary, frustrated by their union leadership, have begun circulating petitions for a free vote on the wage cut proposal.
But Hargrove said most workers, who include those based in Toronto and Vancouver, supported the union leadership's view that 10 percent wage cuts were not a solution to Canadian's financial woes.
"Overall, we'll have an overwhelming vote here to reject this further cut," he said.
Meanwhile, no agreement had been reached by Wednesday between Canadian and AMR, parent of American Airlines, on fee concessions, but intense talks were continuing, said AMR spokesman Al Becker.
Becker repeated, however, that AMR was not interested in infusing Canadian with cash by boosting its stake. AMR has a 33 percent stake in Canadian.
